The Superb fruit dove (Ptilinopus superbus) emerges from the egg at a remarkably modest size, with newly hatched nestlings weighing approximately 7.1 grams [Ww0 = approximately 7.1 grams]. This initial wet weight, recorded from captive-bred individuals, places the species among the smaller-bodied columbids at the point of hatching. The incubation period, during which the embryonated egg is maintained at a relatively cool temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], lasts for 14 days [ab = 14 days], a duration that is notably brief compared to many other members of the Columbidae family. This rapid embryonic development is likely an adaptation that minimizes the vulnerability of the single-egg clutch to predation and stochastic environmental events in its rainforest habitat. The nestling chick, entirely dependent on crop milk and regurgitated fruit pulp from both parents during its first days, begins to gain mass quickly, initiating a growth trajectory that will eventually differentiate markedly between the sexes as they approach adulthood. The single egg, laid in a simple platform nest of twigs, represents a substantial maternal investment for a bird of this size, and the brief incubation period reduces the window of exposure to egg predators such as snakes and arboreal mammals that are common throughout the Australasian rainforest canopy.

Under captive conditions that reflect the thermal environment of their active metabolic periods, maintained at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], the developmental milestones of the Superb fruit dove follow a condensed schedule. The fledgling achieves its first flight and departs the nest at just 7 days after hatching [tx = 7 days after hatching], an exceptionally short nestling period for a pigeon of its adult proportions at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This abbreviated period of dependency is thought to be an anti-predator strategy, reducing the time that the conspicuous nest and vocal, begging chick are exposed. Following this rapid nest departure, the young bird continues to be provisioned by its parents for a short interval as a fledgling, during which it refines its flight skills and learns to identify ripe fruits. Despite this early physical independence, the onset of full reproductive competence is deferred, as the bird must first complete its somatic growth before it can allocate resources toward the production of its own clutch.

Once the juvenile bird attains its adult dimensions, a pronounced sexual size dimorphism becomes evident. The ultimate wet weight achieved by females, representing their asymptotic body mass, averages 112.5 grams [Wwi = 112.5 grams], whereas males are consistently heavier, attaining an average ultimate wet weight of 121.5 grams [Wwi = 121.5 grams]. This difference, a roughly eight percent disparity in body mass, is typical of many fruit-dove species and may be linked to differences in the energetic demands of reproduction versus male-male competition for breeding territories and access to fruiting trees. The larger body size of males likely confers an advantage in agonistic encounters and during the defense of productive foraging patches. Both sexes must reach their full structural size before the hormonal changes that initiate reproductive activation can proceed, a delay that reflects the physiological priority given to somatic growth over reproductive effort during the early post-fledging period.

The timing of sexual maturation in the Superb fruit dove, observed under the stable thermal conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], occurs at 21 days since birth [tp = 21 days since birth], a remarkably early onset of puberty relative to the species' eventual adult size and longevity. This rapid attainment of gonadal maturity suggests that the species is adapted for high turnover and quick replacement in a productive tropical environment, though it does not immediately translate into breeding. Instead, a period of behavioral and physiological preparation follows, during which the young adult establishes a territory and forges a pair bond. The first successful brood, marking the initiation of an individual's reproductive career, is deferred considerably and is observed at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This year-long delay between puberty and first reproduction is a critical life-history bottleneck, allowing the bird to accumulate the necessary experience and energetic reserves to support the single-egg clutch that defines its reproductive strategy.

The reproductive output of the Superb fruit dove is characterized by a conservative strategy, with females laying just a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and producing only one such clutch each year [F_R_i = one such clutch each year]. This low annual fecundity is offset by a relatively prolonged lifespan, with the maximum documented longevity in captivity reaching approximately 15.9 years [am = approximately 15.9 years] when maintained at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This extended lifespan, unusual for a bird of its body size, reduces the risk of population decline even with minimal annual recruitment. The energetic cost of this slow life history is reflected in the species' basal metabolic rate, measured as an oxygen consumption of 136 milliliters per hour [JOi = 136 milliliters per hour] at 40.5 °C at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This metabolic rate, while modest in absolute terms, is consistent with the frugivorous diet and relatively sedentary lifestyle typical of rainforest pigeons, where energy-rich fruits are seasonally available but require significant foraging effort to locate and defend.
